definition: The assumption that training and test data are independent and identically distributed.
details: The assumption that training and test data are independent and identically distributed. Most ML theory rests on it; most production failures happen because it is violated (see Distribution Shift).

explainer.lead: The i.i.d. assumption says training and test data are independent and identically distributed. It matters because most ML theory rests on it, and most production failures happen when it is violated.

tiers.eli5: Like assuming today's weather will follow the same pattern as the weather you studied last year.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers rely on it when estimating generalization from held-out data. The pitfall is deploying on data that drifts from training, a violation known as distribution shift.
tiers.paperLevel: Training and test data are independent and identically distributed. Most ML theory rests on it; violations, called distribution shift, account for most production failures.

explainer.example: A model trained on last year's customer records fails when buying behavior shifts, because the test data is no longer identically distributed to the training data.
